article_text:
With the flesh-hungry cannibal siblings of Raw (2016) and the murderous, androgynous mechanophile of Titane (2021), filmmaker Julia Ducournau injected fresh blood into New French Extremity. The heroines of these films exist in a liminal place amid sex, fear, and death, with their fantastical dimensions cleverly reifying our basest instincts toward the Other. Ducournau’s third theatrical feature, Alpha , which premiered in the main competition of the Cannes Film Festival last year, continues her erotic/thanatic preoccupations and penchant for the surreal, but the movie feels surprisingly grounded. The disease plaguing the world in Alpha may turn people into marble and make them bleed dust, but every other element of the conceit unearths the real history of the AIDS epidemic: the infection spreads via needles and sex, and is clouded in taboo; the patients are ostracized, and decimated, by an uncaring society. The horrors of this film are not as much on the screen as in the painful history it highlights.

This being a Julia Ducournau film, there is a coming-of-age story at the center of this crisis. The 13-year-old Alpha (Mélissa Boros) is trying to make sense of puberty—desire, rebellion, femininity—in an environment suffused with paranoia. Her mother, played by Golshifteh Farahani, is a doctor who toils at the local hospital to try and save the afflicted, even as most of her colleagues have abandoned their posts; meanwhile, Alpha’s uncle, Amin (Tahar Rahim), makes a sudden appearance, his body wrecked by substance abuse and, eventually, the marbling disease. The film is set in an unspecified time in an unspecified location, and as it proceeds, Ducournau blurs and scrambles the chronology. Flashes of the past start to mix in with the present, so that memory and reality become indistinguishable, evoking the workings of collective and familial grief, and the challenge of letting go of someone whom the world never mourned.

With Alpha playing in theaters in New York, I chatted with Ducournau about the film’s key themes: the body, empathy, beauty, and loss.

You’ve spoken about how having doctors for parents shaped your approach to the body. I was fascinated to discover what your parents’ specializations are—is it true that your mom’s a gynecologist and your dad’s a dermatologist?

Absolutely.

Those fields relate in very specific ways to the themes of your films, like gender and reproduction, as well as the skin and the flesh. What did you see growing up that made an impression on you?

If you have doctor parents, you always have magazines and books, so I’ve seen some stuff, especially on the dermatology aspect, that triggered my imagination. But I think that what I keep with me the most is the fact that, in their jobs, there is a constant sense of doubt. We understand why they have to have a cold approach to mortality, to death in general, and to the transformation of the body. But at the same time, this constant questioning implies a great sense of empathy. My parents always told me there is one case per patient, which means that everyone is unique and everyone reacts differently under the same circumstances.

Besides the obvious link with bodily transformation, I think the deep core topic of all my films is unconditional love. How, despite the most dreadful circumstances, there is a place to love someone else, whether they are linked to you or not. And it’s especially in dreadful circumstances—the ones that we are living now or the ones that were happening in the ’90s, as in the case of the film—that this empathy becomes a moral duty.

Something wonderful about the film is that you’re experiencing those events of the ’90s through the eyes of a 13-year-old, who sees things all around her that she does not fully understand. I was wondering if there are certain things you remember about the AIDS crisis from when you were young that left an impression on you, and made their way into the film?

During the peak of the AIDS pandemic, I was between 8 and 15, something like that. What I remember is that no one knew what they were talking about. It wasn’t just that I was young. I felt a total sense of incapacity to take it in, to embrace it, and accept the situation. There was a lot of denial. I also remember the big trauma that was left upon the way we discovered sexuality as teenagers at the time. That impacted my generation very much because we were educated by society that sex was danger. Sex was not healthy. Sex meant that you were doing something profoundly wrong, something very taboo that could kill you or kill someone else. If you think about it, the ’70s were only 20 years prior. We were at the peak of sexual equality and sexual liberation, and it went down in a snap of a finger because of fear and because this huge trauma was never, ever acknowledged.

This denial was made obvious by the fact that the entire world blamed a very specific population and their lifestyle, and decided that they were the scapegoats for this. That was already there. You could feel it. I remember homophobia, xenophobia, as well as acute racism being at a huge peak. Those memories inspired the scene in the classroom where an aggressive student uses a slur to talk to someone he should have respect for—that is, his teacher. One thing that is strange is, I’ve toured a lot already with the film, and I notice that in my younger audiences, some people use the word “dystopian” for that scene. It was actually pretty common and banal. It’s quite a shock to hear that people think that my movie could be set in the future. I always answer that this scene proves that it’s set in the ’90s.

There was a line in the press notes that I really loved. You said you would have felt “it blasphemous to portray the factual symptoms of AIDS, knowing that people would come to the film expecting to be repelled. I wanted to create the opposite reaction.” That made me think about what a clever choice it was to choose marbling as the manifestation of the disease in your film, because it is scary to think of turning into stone, but stone sculptures are also symbols of beauty in art.

To me, the marble represents something more like sanctity. Marble is usually used for saints in cathedrals, and to portray people who are beyond us. So it became a way to elevate to something saintly the lives and the deaths of the people who were deemed less than human. It’s not religious; it’s more my way of trying to hint at a form of reparation, to find dignity and respect for them.

Make them martyrs.

Exactly. At first I thought, I want people to see them as beautiful and I want to make them beautiful. That was naïve because the concept of beauty is never objective. What I find beautiful, people might find repellent. So my take on what’s beautiful was irrelevant, and I could not base the iconography of my film on that.

When I wrote the scene in the waiting room, where Alpha runs into her teacher and his companion, and says “you’re beautiful,” I projected myself into directing the actress and I thought, you have got to tell her that she really means it. It’s not because she’s being polite. We see this from the beginning of the scene because she’s just fascinated by the way he looks; she just stares at him like you would stare at Michelangelo’s Pietà. So when I wrote that, I realized that as long as she sees him as beautiful, everyone will. Her point of view matters more than my point of view.

I know that you are partly of Berber descent.

Yeah, my mom is Berber.

Did you know from the beginning that this would be set in a Berber family?

It was important to me in many ways, because the film is so much about the persistence of love—the strength it can give you, and also the fact that it can generate so much fear in you. As I said before at the beginning of our conversation, unconditional love was something that I wanted to portray very frontally, which was a first for me. In Titane it only happens in the last 15 minutes of the film.

I was struck by the dinner scene, when Alpha, her mother, and her aunts and uncles are all at the grandma’s house. It was so joyful! I don’t think your other films have had a scene like that, which is just so full of… light?

That is what our lunches or dinners looked like in my family during my childhood. This big chaos, this big matriarchy, where women talk more than men, and take a lot of space, and handle everything. There are petty arguments that are overcome by laughter two seconds later, and the just nonstop food coming and nonstop jokes coming.

The question of the family being Berber—it was natural to me knowing that in this film I would have to be more up-front than I had ever been as far as the expression of love and family were concerned. In Titane , my two characters are archetypical figures. I thought about them as gods, Uranus and Gaia. In this film, it’s only raw humanity, no demigods. It’s closer to my experience.

There was never any political aspect to the representation of this family. I noticed afterward that I was asked about it very much, and it left me disturbed. I wondered how much, when you represent a family that is not the standard white family, people need it to be a social or political agenda.

Can you talk about the concept of the “red wind” in the film? Both the idea behind it and the look. It affects the color palette of the film, there’s this beautiful red glow.

There are two things. The first is logical, and the second is about its interpretation. The reason it’s red stems from the scene where Amin’s back disintegrates while Alpha’s mother is examining it. For when the dust starts trickling down, there was the question of what color it would be. Is it white, like you would expect marble to be, or is it red, as you would expect blood to be if it’s calcified? I chose red because if it had been white, then I would have made the patients statues, something that was no longer human. By keeping the blood red and just making it calcified, I keep his humanity.

I’m cautious about imposing my interpretation, because, to start with, it is different from my characters’ interpretation. To the grandma, the red wind represents disease. It represents a form of demon. It’s not that to me at all. To me, it’s about how you keep in your skin the memory of the people that you’ve lost. The wind wipes the hurt away, but at the same time, the dust lingers. It says something about the fact that grieving changes your state of being in the world. Once you’ve lost someone you loved, you mutate into another state of being. But I’m worried about explaining this, because I believe that this is open to anyone’s interpretation and their own experience of grief.

The closing scene, with the storm of red wind, is stunning. I don’t want to spoil it, but it made me think about how grief is a way of insisting that someone or something was real. It’s scary to stop grieving because you fear that if you let go, they won’t exist anymore in the world.

That scene was a big thing because we covered this entire neighborhood in a big layer of red dust, made of red bricks that were crushed. For the production designer [Emmanualle Duplay] and her crew, it took them a week to do that. It was absolutely insane. We also played with big fans in order to have this wind, and this dust coming up. So it was, as is everything that I do, 50 percent practical and 50 percent CGI.

What you said about the scene is very beautiful. That’s exactly why I do not want to impose too much on the interpretation, because you just said something that is very true, through the prism of your own experience, your own subjectivity.
excerpt_original: Unconditional loves: the French director discusses her latest, a surreal and moving coming-of-age story that reimagines the AIDS crisis

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Colman Domingo , Jeff Goldblum , Rachel McAdams and David Krumholtz have boarded Benny Safdie ‘s Lizard Music in voice roles.

The Amazon MGM Studios’ and United Artists’ (UA) live-action/CGI hybrid film cast also includes previously announced star and producer Dwayne Johnson, Theo Leber, Alicia Silverstone, Tim Heidecker, Arya Parvathi, Regina Hall and Andrew Dice Clay.

Related Stories

Regina Hall Joins Dwayne Johnson In Benny Safdie’s ‘Lizard Music’ From United Artists And Amazon MGM Studios

Alicia Silverstone & Tim Heidecker Latest To Join Benny Safdie’s ‘Lizard Music’

The film will follow a boy (Leber), left to his own devices, who stumbles upon a secret late-night broadcast of lizards playing otherworldly music. Thus, a hidden door to the extraordinary swings open. Leber’s search for answers leads him to an eccentric and whimsical old man nicknamed The Chicken Man (Johnson), and his beloved companion, an 85 year-old chicken named Claudia. The boy and the old man become two kindred spirits who found each other at just the right time.

United by a shared vision, they set off on an adventure that begins as a hunt for a hidden society but blossoms into something far greater: a voyage through invisible worlds, unexpected harmonies, and the unbreakable bond between lost souls who discover magic not only in what they find, but in each other.

Watch on Deadline

Safdie wrote the script, which is based on the Daniel Pinkwater novel of the same name.

Producers include UA’s Scott Stuber and Nick Nesbitt, Out for the Count Productions’ Benny Safdie, Seven Bucks Productions’ Dwayne Johnson and Magnetic Fields Entertainment’s David Koplan.

Two-time Academy Award nominee Domingo has won an Emmy, NAACP Image and Gotham Award. His recent film work includes portraying Joe Jackson in Antoine Fuqua’s Michael and starring in Steven Spielberg’s Disclosure Day alongside Emily Blunt. This weekend he will be honored at The Academy Museum Gala with their Vantage Award. Previously, he starred in and executive produced Sing Sing , directed by Greg Kwedar, earning Academy Award, Golden Globe, Bafta, Critics Choice, and SAG nominations for the role. On television, Domingo recently starred in Season 3 of HBO’s Euphoria and Season 2 of Netflix’s The Four Seasons , earning 2026 Emmy Award nominations for both performances. Upcoming is Jaume Collet-Serra’s Netflix series An Innocent Girl .

RELATED: Dwayne Johnson Describes ‘Lizard Music’ As “‘Willy Wonka’ From The Mind Of Benny Safdie,” Details 5-Hour Makeup Process To Play 70-Year-Old — D23

Domingo is co-writing an original live-action Princess Tiana movie for Disney, inspired by the 2009 animated film The Princess and The Frog . He also led the limited series The Madness , created by Clement Virgo. In 2024, he voiced Norman Osborn in the Disney+ animated series Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man . He is also attached to star and executive produce “Headlands House”, a thriller limited series in development at Netflix. Domingo is represented by Liebman Entertainment, WME, Schreck Rose Dapello Adams Berlin and W|K Public Relations.

Recently co-starring as The Wizard of Oz with Ariana Grande and Cynthia Erivo in the Jon M. Chu’s Wicked and Wicked: For Good , Jeff Goldblum is an Oscar-nominated director for his short feature film, Little Surprises . Goldblum’s film credits include The Big Chill, The Grand Budapest Hotel , The Fly , Independence Day , Jurassic Park , and Thor: Ragnarok. For television, he has been Emmy nominated for his work on Will and Grace and for his National Geographic/Disney+ offering The World According to Jeff Goldblum , which he also executive produced. Jeff Goldblum is represented by CAA, Constellation Media Group and Hansen, Jacobson, Teller.

Rachel McAdams was nominated for an Academy Award for her role as Sacha Pfeiffer in the 2015 film, Spotlight, directed by Tom McCarthy. McAdams most recently starred in the 20th Century Studios film Send Help alongside Dylan O’Brien, which was released earlier this year. Rachel McAdams is represented by Magnolia, WME, Narrative and Howard Fishman.

David Krumholtz was most recently seen in DC Studios’ Supergirl and will next be seen in Paramount’s football underdog story Mr. Irrelevant , out Christmas Day. Krumholtz starred in the Academy Award-winning feature Oppenheimer for Universal Pictures. Additional film credits include the Bruce Springsteen biopic Deliver Me From Nowhere, Bob Byington’s Lousy Carter, Down With The King , The Coen Brothers’ The Ballad Of Buster Scruggs and Hail Caesar!, I Saw The Light, The Judge , This Is The End , Sausage Party, Oliver Irving’s Ghost Team, Superbad, Columbia Pictures’ Walk Hard, and Universal’s Oscar-winning Ray . Television credits include CBS’ NUMB3RS, The Santa Clause, The Deuce , Apple TV+’s The Studio, The Plot Against America, and The White House Plumbers. Krumholtz is represented by Paradigm, Untitled, and Sloane, Offer, Weber & Dern.

article_text:
Zeitz MOCAA welcomes a new, site-specific commission by Ghanaian-American artist Rita Mawuena Benissan. The Procession (2025), the large-scale cylindrical tapestry made of sheer fabric and embroidered canvas, invokes a space for convening and celebration. The Atrium commission opened on 25 October 2025 and will be on view intil 25 October 2026.

Benissan’s artistic practice is rooted in the cultural traditions of Ghanaian royalty, where public processions honour chiefs and traditional leaders. These processions are vibrant occasions marked by canopies of dancing royal umbrellas, colourful attire, and the rhythmic pulse of drumming. The Procession embodies the essence of this tradition through its vivid use of colour, its depiction of community, and motifs of seagulls and palm fronds spanning the full height of the Atrium.

Suspended at the centre of the Atrium bowl, the permeable tapestry takes the form of a delicate apparition that softens its rough, concrete surroundings. Its presence ethereal and monumental, an elegant halo responding to the atmosphere of the space—the quiet stir of an incoming breeze, the shifting light, the indistinct chatter of the visitors. The Procession invites reflection on community, and the rich Ghanaian traditions that sustain it. Here at the museum, it becomes a moment for collective gathering—a procession in its own right—as visitors move through and around the work.

Contributors to The Procession :

Idris Tanko (Lead) Travis Obeng-Casper (Lead) Carl Gomado (Lead) Toffic Zakaria Faisal Husain Mamud Tahiru Sadat Anwar Husain Alhssan Nasir Saeed Suleman Bawa Humphrey Abbey Noah Teye Kofi Dako

Zeitz MOCAA’s exhibition and curatorial programming is generously supported by the Mellon Foundation and BMW South Africa. This commission has been made possible through the generous support of Gallery 1957.

meet the artist

rita mawuena benissan

Portrait by Lauren Theunissen, courtesy of Zeitz MOCAA.

Rita Mawuena Benissan , a Ghanaian-American interdisciplinary artist, is on a mission to reimagine the royal umbrella, transforming it from a mere protective object into a potent symbol of Ghanaian identity. With a profound passion for art and cultural history, Benissan collaborates with traditional artisans to breathe life into archival photos, immortalising individual figures and communal scenes while embodying the beauty and power of her people.

Born in Abidjan, Côte D’Ivoire in 1995 to Ghanaian parents, Benissan’s journey led her to the United States as a baby, where she earned a Bachelor of Fine Arts in Apparel and Textile Design from Michigan State University (2017), followed by a Master of Fine Arts in Photography, and an African Studies Program Certificate from the University of Wisconsin-Madison (2021).

In 2020, Benissan established Si Hene, a foundation dedicated to preserving Ghana’s chieftaincy and traditional culture, leaving a significant mark on Ghana’s artistic and historical narratives. Through her foundation, she played a pivotal role in the reopening of the National Museum of Ghana in 2022 and served as the Chief Curator at the Institute Museum of Ghana (Noldor Artist Residency) until 2022. She also acted as Artistic Director for the Open Society Foundation’s Restitution Conference in Accra, demonstrating her commitment to cultural preservation and representation.

Benissan’s artistic prowess has garnered global recognition, with exhibitions at prestigious venues such as Arts + Literature Laboratory, Wisconsin (2021); the Foundation for Contemporary Art at Afrochella Festival, Accra (2021), Dak’Art – Biennale de l’Art Africain Contemporain at IFAN African Art Museum, Dakar (2022), EFIE: Museum as Home, Dortmund (2023), and Mitchell-Innes & Nash, New York (2023). Her solo exhibition, In the World Not of the World , curated by Ekow Eshun at Gallery 1957, Accra (2023), stands as a testament to her unwavering dedication to redefining the narrative of Ghanaian identity. Recent presentations include 1-54 Marrakesh (2024), alongside Amoako Boafo and Zanele Muholi; Unapologetic WomXn: The Dream is the Truth , curated by Destinee Ross Sutton at the Venice Biennale (2024); and the Sharjah Biennale (2024).

Building on the milestone of being the subject of her first museum exhibition at Zeitz MOCAA, she was commissioned for a landmark installation in the museum’s Atrium in November 2025, becoming the first woman and youngest artist to undertake this prestigious project.

Benissan’s work is represented in numerous private and institutional collections, including Foundation H, The Dean Collection, The OmenaArt Foundation, Fundación Yannick y Ben, Paola Pavirani Golinelli, Nicolas Berggruen, Amoako Boafo, among others.

Image credit: Installation view, The Procession . Photo: Slater Studio, courtesy of Zeitz MOCAA.

article_text:
Lynn Painter ’s Fake Skating novel will become a movie to be released in theaters next year.

The news was first reported by Deadline before that of Painter’s Better Than The Movies film adaptation , which is in the works at Netflix . While hockey, figure skating and other romances set in the rink have largely been taking place on streamers, this one will make it to the big screen.

Related Stories

Everything We Know About Netflix’s ‘Better Than The Movies’ Feature Adaptation So Far

‘Fake Skating’ Feature Adaptation At Sony Taps Amélie Hoeferle and Graham Campbell To Star

For everything we know about the movie adaptation of Lynn Painter’s Fake Skating book, read on.

Watch on Deadline

When will the Fake Skating movie come out?

The film is slated to arrive in theaters via Sony Pictures July 16, 2027.

Who will be in the cast of the Fake Skating movie?

Deadline first reported that Amélie Hoeferle ( Sterling Point, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes ) and Graham Campbell ( The Shards, Late Fame ) will star as the lead couple — Dani and Alec — in the film.

What is Lynn Painter’s Fake Skating about?

The high school hockey romance sees childhood sweethearts experience a cold reunion in their hometown, which loves hockey. They thaw things when they enter a fake dating relationship, as predicted by the book’s title.

RELATED: Julia Hart Directing Feature Adaptation Of Lynn Painter’s Bestselling YA Rom-Com Novel ‘Better Than The Movies’ For Netflix

Who is directing the Fake Skating movie?

Deadline broke the news that Josh Boone, who recently directed Paramount’s adaptation of Colleen Hoover’s best-selling book Regretting You , starring Allison Williams, Dave Franco, Mason Thames and McKenna Grace, will helm Fake Skating . He also directed the film adaptation of John Green’s The Fault in Our Stars .

Who else is behind the Fake Skating movie?

The screenplay was penned by Morgan Lehmann and Victoria Bata with Boone and his writing partner Knate Lee handling revisions.

Will Gluck’s ( Anyone But You , One Night Only ) Olive Bridge Entertainment is producing the film. Gluck and Jacqueline Monetta are producing, and Madison Jones is executive producing on behalf of Olive Bridge Entertainment. Painter will also serve as an executive producer.

日本のコンテンポラリーアートシーンに新たな視点を提示してきたアーティスト、YOSHIROTTEN。 TOKYO NODE では、彼の過去最大規模となる個展 「ヨシロットン展 彼方との交信／BEYOND EARTH」 が、10月30日から2027年1月11日まで開催されています。 グラフィックデザイン、アートディレクション、映像、演出、空間設計など多岐にわたる領域で活動し、カルチャーを横断しながら独自の視覚言語を確立してきたYOSHIROTTEN。本展では、地上約200mに位置するTOKYO NODEをひとつの「宇宙船」に見立て、「見えないものの可視化」をテーマに据えた大規模なインスタレーションを展開、身体では知覚できない「彼方」と出会うような体験を生み出します。

「宇宙船」に見立てた地上200mのギャラリーで変化し続ける展覧会。会期は10月30日〜2027年1月11日

本展のチケットをTokyo Art Beatの有料会員限定で、抽選で5組10名様にプレゼントします。

article_text:
冨永愛の伝統to未来 第二章～ニッポンの伝統文化を未来へ紡ぐ～

サブタイトル：鎚起銅器②（ついきどうき）

放送日時：2026年11月4日(水)夜10時～10時30分

放送局：BS日テレ

出演者：冨永愛

クレジット：ⒸＢＳ日テレ

番組概要:冨永愛が全国各地を訪ね、その土地に根付く「伝統文化」を紹介します。先人たちから受け継がれてきた「伝統」の素晴らしさを伝えるとともに、後継者問題など伝統文化が置かれている「現状」、そして進むべき「未来」を探っていきます。

番組ホームページ： https://www.bs4.jp/dentotomirai/ 番組公式X： https://x.com/dentou_mirai 番組公式Youtube: https://www.youtube.com/@dentoumirai 番組公式TikTok： https://www.tiktok.com/@dentoumirai 番組公式インスタグラム： https://www.instagram.com/bs4_dentou_mirai/

愛さんの豆皿、その仕上がりは？

前回に引き続き、一枚の銅板を金槌で叩き打ち縮めることで、立体的な器へと仕上げる伝統工芸・「鎚起銅器（ついきどうき）」を紹介します。 「金属産業のまち」新潟県燕市で200年以上の歴史を持つ「玉川堂」を訪れ、その魅力を探っていきます。 そして、前回から挑戦している愛さんの豆皿もいよいよ完成。 玉川堂の着色技術で職人も驚く仕上がりに。 どんな豆皿になったのか、お楽しみに！

独自の着色技法の秘密に迫る

そんな玉川堂独自の色は、銅の表面に錫を焼き付けた後、硫化カリウム等の液に漬け込むことで生まれます。 実は大正時代、作業中偶然に発見されたというその着色技法に迫ります。 さらに終業後、工場を職人に開放し、若手の技術訓練やベテランの作品創作にチャレンジする場として提供しています。 そんな、未来を担う職人さんたちが作る作品の数々を紹介。

オープンファクトリーの先駆け

そして、番頭を務める山田立さんは、日本のオープンファクトリーの先駆けともいわれる「燕三条 工場の祭典」の立ち上げから関わり、実行委員長も務めてきた人物。 工場の祭典は地域の工場を一斉開放して、ものづくりのまち燕三条の魅力を体感してもらう産業観光イベント。150を超える企業が参加し、過去には6万2千人を動員しました。 さらに、参加する工房や工場が工場の祭典をきっかけに業績を伸ばしています。

工場の祭典はなぜ日本を代表するオープンファクトリーとなったのか？ 参加している工房や立ち上げから携わる山田さんにその理由をお聞きします。 さらに「燕三条 工場の祭典 2026」にも密着！その様子をお届けします。 (美術展ナビ編集班)

article_text:
見上げてごらん

劇場公開日： 2026年10月30日

映画館を探す

予告編を見る

映画チケットを U-NEXTでお得にゲット PR

解説・あらすじ

森田剛が主演を務め、マンガの制作現場を舞台に万年アシスタントの中年男性の奮闘を軽やかにつづったヒューマンドラマ。 巨匠マンガ家のアシスタントを長年にわたり務めてきた、42歳の土屋輝一。マンガ家デビューした後輩や人気声優である別居中の妻に対してモヤモヤした思いを抱え、一緒に暮らす高校受験生の娘とも気持ちがすれ違ってばかりいる。そんな彼のもとに、あるマンガ企画が舞い込む。仕事への熱量不足を自覚する29歳の中堅編集者・潮田ユキと、マンガ家を志す猪突猛進な40歳の新人アシスタント・山田ぽてとと共に、マンガ制作に踏み出す土屋だったが……。 編集者・潮田ユキ役で森川葵、新人アシスタント・山田ぽてと役で川上友里、潮田の上司である編集部長・馬場明役で阿部寛、土屋の別居中の妻・莉花役で松本まりか、土屋がアシスタントを務める巨匠マンガ家・吉住はるを役で武田鉄矢、土屋の娘・ひかり役で早瀬憩が共演。監督は、是枝裕和監督作の助監督などを務めてきた森本晶一と、「泣く子はいねぇが」の佐藤快磨。是枝監督率いる映像制作者集団「分福」に所属する両監督が共同監督を務め、森本監督が自身の経験に着想を得て原案・オリジナル脚本を手がけた。

title_original: Mona Hatoum racconta la sua ricerca alla Fondazione Prada di Milano
editorial_title_zh: Mona Hatoum 在米兰普拉达基金会讲述其创作探索
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在米兰普拉达基金会的展览举办之际，Mona Hatoum 将与公众见面并带来一场讲座，专门探讨她跨越行为艺术、录像、雕塑与装置的创作探索。本文源自……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mona Hatoum 将于2026年10月28日星期三下午18时30分在米兰普拉达基金会（Fondazione Prada）出席一场公众见面会。这场讲座将在戈达尔影院（Cinema Godard）举行，并为艺术家目前正在该基金会米兰馆址举办的个人展览《Over, under and in between》拉开序幕，展期将持续至9月。", "links": [{"text": "Milano", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/tag/milano/"}, {"text": "Over, under and in between", "url": "https://www.fondazioneprada.org/project/exhibition-mona-hatoum-over-under-and-in-between/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "此次活动开启了普拉达基金会为其在米兰和威尼斯馆址举办的展览及正在进行的项目所推出的一系列全新讲座、对话与深度探讨，活动将邀请艺术家、策展人及其他当代文化界人士共同参与。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Mona Hatoum 讲述自己的创作探索", "translated": true}, {"type": article_text:
Mona Hatoum sarà protagonista di un incontro pubblico alla Fondazione Prada di Milano , mercoledì, 28 ottobre 2026, alle ore 18:30. La lecture si svolgerà al Cinema Godard e accompagnerà Over, under and in between , la mostra personale dell’artista in corso nella sede milanese della Fondazione fino al 9 novembre.

L’appuntamento inaugura una nuova serie di incontri, conversazioni e approfondimenti che Fondazione Prada dedica alle mostre e ai progetti in corso nelle sedi di Milano e Venezia, coinvolgendo artisti, curatori e altre figure della cultura contemporanea.

Mona Hatoum racconta la propria ricerca

Nel corso della lecture, Hatoum ripercorrerà le principali fasi della propria pratica artistica, soffermandosi sui temi che ne hanno segnato la ricerca fin dagli esordi: sradicamento, marginalizzazione, esclusione, controllo sociale e politico, ma anche corpo, vulnerabilità e rapporto con lo spazio.

L’incontro sarà accompagnato dalla proiezione di due opere video appartenenti alla prima fase del suo percorso: Measures of Distance del 1988, della durata di circa 15 minuti, e Roadworks del 1985, lavoro di poco meno di sette minuti. Si tratta di due opere legate agli anni in cui la pratica di Hatoum era maggiormente concentrata sulla performance e sul video, prima del progressivo passaggio, a partire dagli anni Novanta, verso installazioni e sculture di grande scala.

Over, under and in between: tre installazioni per la Cisterna

L’incontro si inserisce nel programma della mostra Over, under and in between , progetto site specific concepito da Hatoum per gli spazi della Cisterna di Fondazione Prada e aperto dallo scorso 29 gennaio. La mostra si articola in tre installazioni costruite attorno ad altrettanti elementi ricorrenti nel vocabolario dell’artista: la ragnatela, la mappa e la griglia. Le opere occupano le tre sale dell’edificio, sfruttandone altezza, volume e struttura per costruire un percorso incentrato su instabilità, pericolo e fragilità.

Nella prima sala, una costellazione di sfere di vetro trasparente sospese e collegate da fili forma una grande ragnatela, immagine insieme protettiva e minacciosa. Nello spazio centrale, oltre 30mila sfere di vetro rosso compongono una mappa del mondo priva di confini politici, costruita secondo la proiezione Gall-Peters e lasciata intenzionalmente in uno stato di precarietà.

L’ultima sala ospita invece all of a quiver , installazione cinetica alta 8,6 metri costituita da nove livelli di strutture cubiche metalliche. Attivata da un sistema motorizzato, la griglia oscilla lentamente tra collasso e ricostruzione, trasformando una struttura geometrica rigida in un organismo instabile e in continuo movimento.

Attraverso queste tre opere, Hatoum costruisce un rapporto diretto tra corpo del visitatore e spazio espositivo, alternando attrazione e disagio, familiarità e minaccia.

Mona Hatoum, una ricerca tra corpo, politica e spazio

Nata a Beirut nel 1952 da una famiglia palestinese, Mona Hatoum vive a Londra dal 1975. Lo scoppio della guerra civile libanese le impedì in quell’anno di fare ritorno in Libano, mentre si trovava nel Regno Unito.

La sua ricerca si è sviluppata attraverso performance, video, fotografia, scultura, installazione e lavori su carta. Negli anni Ottanta Hatoum si è fatta conoscere soprattutto attraverso azioni e video incentrati sul corpo, utilizzato come luogo di conflitto, vulnerabilità e resistenza. A partire dagli anni Novanta, la sua pratica si è orientata sempre più verso oggetti, ambienti e installazioni capaci di trasformare forme apparentemente familiari in presenze ambigue o minacciose.

Griglie, utensili domestici, mappe, mobili, strutture architettoniche e oggetti quotidiani vengono spesso alterati nelle dimensioni, nei materiali o nella funzione, generando una tensione continua tra attrazione e repulsione, protezione e pericolo.

Hatoum ha partecipato ad alcune delle principali rassegne internazionali, tra cui la Biennale di Venezia nel 1995 e nel 2005, documenta a Kassel nel 2002 e nel 2017, la Biennale di Sydney, la Biennale di Sharjah e la Biennale di Taipei. Tra le sue mostre personali più rilevanti figura la retrospettiva organizzata nel 2015 dal Centre Pompidou di Parigi e successivamente presentata alla Tate Modern di Londra e al KIASMA di Helsinki. Più recentemente, nel 2025, il Barbican Centre di Londra ha messo in dialogo il suo lavoro con quello di Alberto Giacometti nella mostra Encounters: Giacometti x Mona Hatoum .

Nel corso della carriera l’artista ha ricevuto, tra gli altri, il Joan Miró Prize nel 2011, l’Hiroshima Art Prize nel 2017, il Praemium Imperiale per la scultura nel 2019 e il Premio Julio González nel 2020.

article_text:
À travers sa série De l’autre côté , Anouchka Clot a suivi Saï dans son parcours de transition de genre. Un travail construit et pensé à deux, permettant d’archiver et de témoigner de l’intérieur, ce qui se joue dans la chair.

Artiste auteure photographe installée à Clermont-Ferrand, Anouchka Clot découvre la photographie numérique à l’âge de 15 ans, grâce à son frère aîné. Là, déjà, le médium permet de faire lien, à soi, au monde et aux autres. C’est une source de transmission, une manière de se relier et d’observer. Puis vient la photographie argentique , et, avec elle, un rapport au temps retrouvé, une place laissée au hasard et à l’erreur, aux zones d’ombres, comme à celles de lumière. Une façon aussi pour Anouchka Clot de mettre au cœur le geste, de développer et de tirer ses images, d’attendre que les choses se fassent dans la lenteur. « J’ai pu, grâce à la photographie argentique, développer mon rapport au lâcher-prise et à la confiance qui m’ont toujours semblé difficiles à mobiliser d’ordinaire. L’argentique me permet aussi de travailler mon rapport au deuil ; ce n’est pas arrivé au hasard dans ma vie. La création est pour moi un acte artistique autant que politique qui sert de medium à mon introspection et au vivre-ensemble. Mes projets photo visent à mettre en lumière des sujets invisibilisés ou stigmatisés. »

C’est dans cette même dynamique qu’elle réalise, avec son ami Saï, sa série De l’autre côté , traduction du mot latin « trans ». À travers cette série, Anouchka Clot l’a suivi, durant plusieurs années, tout au long de son processus de transition. « Ce projet a été entièrement pensé et construit en partenariat avec lui et c’est un point très important : le sujet de la transidentité ne peut être présenté qu’avec les personnes concernées. Cette codirection artistique était donc primordiale pour éviter l’appropriation de son vécu » , explique-t-elle. Se focalisant d’abord sur le calendrier d’hormonothérapie (traitement médical qui vise à bloquer ou à diminuer l’action des hormones naturelles) de son modèle, et plus précisément de ses prises de testostérone (ou T) tous les 21 jours par injection, elle réalise ses premières images. À mesure que la série se construit, elle s’en éloigne, pour aller vers une approche plus sensible et subjective. Une manière surtout de s’extirper de potentielles représentations stéréotypées de la transidentité et de ne pas retomber dans une iconographie qui enfermerait à nouveau son sujet dans des cases. Une façon de refléter surtout ce qui traverse Saï de l’intérieur, cet aller-retour entre son corps et ce qui le mue. « Nous voulions parler de transidentité sans ramener ce sujet uniquement au travers des modifications corporelles. Nous voulions que ce projet contribue à la diversité des représentations de genre sans en imposer de nouvelles injonctions, ni stéréotypes. Concernant le modèle, il était important pour lui de voir son parcours archivé et de découvrir grâce à l’autre une partie de son reflet. »

Dans la chair

Capturées principalement en noir et blanc pour la dimension intemporelle, les images d’Anouchka Clot forment, une fois assemblées, une sorte « de continuum de la transidentité dans l’histoire, du passé à aujourd’hui » . Surgit parfois de la couleur dans les photographies, comme celles de fruits pourrissant à l’air libre, afin de ramener au cœur le réel, retisser un lien au présent et créer de la profondeur. S’ajoutent à cela des superpositions, où les visages se mêlent aux branchages et aux végétaux. Des façons de révéler la complexité de ce qui se joue dans le processus de transition, le rapport particulier à l’image. Une alternance de procédés comme autant d’émotions divergentes et de choses qui se tapissent dans le silence : cette violence sourde de la société qui rejette et stigmatise. « La population trans connaît aujourd’hui la violence que représente l’espace public et apprend trop souvent à s’adapter ou à invisibiliser une partie ou la totalité de son identité pour se protéger. La double exposition vient faire écho à cette réalité. »

Mais dans les étreintes partagées, les pansements qui collent aux peaux pour les recouvrir, les tatouages qui les marquent pour l’éternité ou dans le sourire de Saï tenant une seringue de T, se logent une force inouïe, un espoir. Un message qui, comme un cri d’humanité ancré dans la chair, nous dit « qu’aucune personne transgenre ne verra sa sécurité, ses droits et son bonheur remis en question par des politiques fascistes et discriminantes. Ici se confie une intimité universelle qui, nous l’espérons, s’ouvrira, et en fera résonner d’autres ».

De l’autre côté sera exposé au Fototras Festival à partir du 19 novembre 2026 à Capesterre-Belle-Eau, en Guadeloupe .
